questions.decisiveClue: The change currently exists in the workspace and must be written outward to the connected Git branch.

questions.title: Resolve a Git conflict by taking the repository version
questions.context: Aurora has conflicting changes to one Fabric item: an uncommitted workspace version and a newer incoming version in Git. Priya decides the Git version is authoritative and selects Accept incoming changes for that item.
questions.question: What is the key consequence?

options.label: The incoming Git version overwrites the conflicting workspace version for that item
options.explanation: Accept incoming changes resolves the conflict by replacing the workspace content with the repository version.

options.label: The workspace version automatically overwrites the Git branch
options.explanation: That would preserve the workspace version rather than accepting the incoming Git version.

options.label: Fabric always merges both versions field by field with no possibility of data loss
options.explanation: Conflict resolution is not guaranteed to perform a semantic field-by-field merge; accepting incoming changes replaces the workspace version.

options.label: The workspace is automatically disconnected from Git
options.explanation: Resolving the conflict does not inherently disconnect the Git integration.

questions.decisiveClue: The user explicitly chooses the incoming repository version as authoritative, so the conflicting workspace content is replaced.

questions.title: Deploy only the items that passed testing
questions.context: Aurora’s Test stage contains ten changed Fabric items. Only three have passed validation and should move to Production today; the other seven must remain unchanged in Production.
questions.question: Which deployment approach should the release manager use?

options.label: Selective deployment of the three approved items
options.explanation: Deployment pipelines support selective deployment so approved items can move without deploying every changed item in the source stage.

options.label: Full deployment of all ten items
options.explanation: Full deployment would also move the seven changes that have not passed validation.

options.label: Commit only three items to Git and assume Production updates automatically
options.explanation: A Git commit does not itself perform the requested Test-to-Production pipeline deployment.

options.label: Change the seven items to Viewer permissions
options.explanation: Permissions do not prevent a full deployment from moving item definitions.

questions.decisiveClue: The release must move a subset of changed items while leaving the rest of Production unchanged.

questions.title: Understand what happens to a paired target item during deployment
questions.context: Aurora has a report paired between Test and Production in a deployment pipeline. The Production copy contains an unapproved manual layout change. The team now deploys the paired Test report to Production.
questions.question: What should they expect for the paired report definition?

options.label: The deployed Test definition overwrites the paired Production item definition
options.explanation: When content is deployed to an existing stage, paired target items are updated from the source stage, so unmanaged target-only changes can be overwritten.

options.label: The Production definition always wins because it is in the later stage
options.explanation: Deployment direction determines which definition is applied; the later stage does not automatically win.

options.label: Fabric guarantees a field-level merge of both report definitions
options.explanation: Deployment is not a guaranteed semantic merge of independently edited target and source definitions.

options.label: Fabric must create a second Production report instead of updating the paired item
options.explanation: Paired items are updated during deployment rather than necessarily duplicated.

questions.decisiveClue: The report is already paired and the deployment is from Test to Production, so the source definition is applied to the target item.

questions.title: Check downstream effects before dropping a warehouse column
questions.context: Aurora plans to drop a Warehouse column used by unknown downstream teams. The owner wants to identify dependent reports, semantic models, and other downstream items before approving the breaking change.
questions.question: What should the owner perform first?

options.label: Impact analysis of downstream dependencies
options.explanation: Impact analysis is designed to reveal downstream items that depend on an analytics asset before a potentially breaking change.

options.label: Refresh the Warehouse
options.explanation: Refreshing data does not identify which downstream assets depend on the column.

options.label: Certify the Warehouse
options.explanation: Certification signals trust and does not enumerate downstream dependencies.

options.label: Revert the latest Git commit
options.explanation: A Git revert changes source-controlled content and is not a dependency-discovery step.

questions.decisiveClue: The decision requires identifying downstream dependencies before a breaking structural change.

questions.title: Distinguish XMLA read access from metadata write operations
questions.context: Nina needs an external tool to connect to a semantic model and run read-only queries. She does not need to deploy metadata changes, process partitions, or alter the model.
questions.question: Which XMLA capability is sufficient for the endpoint behavior itself?

options.label: XMLA read-only access, together with the required model permissions
options.explanation: Read-only XMLA supports querying and browsing without enabling metadata-management write operations.

options.label: XMLA read-write is always required even for read-only queries
options.explanation: Read-write is needed for write-management scenarios, but the scenario explicitly requires only querying.

options.label: A deployment-pipeline rule
options.explanation: Deployment rules do not enable an external client to query a semantic model through XMLA.

options.label: Workspace Admin is the XMLA endpoint mode
options.explanation: Workspace roles and XMLA endpoint modes are different controls.

questions.decisiveClue: The external operation is purely read/query; no model write or management action is required.

questions.title: Propagate product filters to sales facts
questions.context: Aurora has DimProduct with one row per ProductKey and FactSales with many rows per ProductKey. Report users filter by Product attributes and expect those filters to constrain sales measures.
questions.question: Which relationship pattern is the normal star-schema choice?

options.label: A one-to-many relationship from DimProduct to FactSales with filtering from the one side to the many side
options.explanation: A dimension-to-fact one-to-many relationship allows product filters to propagate from the unique dimension row to matching fact rows.

options.label: A direct many-to-many relationship between DimProduct and FactSales
options.explanation: DimProduct has a unique ProductKey, so many-to-many cardinality is unnecessary and less appropriate.

options.label: A single-direction relationship that filters only from FactSales to DimProduct
options.explanation: The common analytical requirement is for dimension selections to filter facts, not the reverse-only direction.

options.label: No relationship; rely on matching column names
options.explanation: Matching names do not create model filter propagation.

questions.decisiveClue: DimProduct has unique ProductKey values while FactSales has repeated ProductKey values, and product selections must filter the facts.

questions.title: Calculate sales by an inactive Ship Date relationship
questions.context: FactSales has OrderDateKey and ShipDateKey, both related to DimDate. The OrderDate relationship is active. The ShipDate relationship is inactive, and Marta needs a Shipped Sales measure that evaluates using ShipDate.
questions.question: Which DAX technique most directly fits?

options.label: Use USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE for the ShipDate relationship
options.explanation: USERELATIONSHIP lets a calculation activate an inactive relationship for the duration of that calculation.

options.label: Change both date relationships to active simultaneously
options.explanation: Power BI permits only one active filter-propagation path between the same two model tables, so both relationships cannot simply be active together in this design.

options.label: Use FORMAT on ShipDateKey
options.explanation: Formatting a key does not activate the inactive relationship.

options.label: Create an RLS role on DimDate
options.explanation: RLS controls row access by identity and does not switch the relationship used by this measure.

questions.decisiveClue: The required calculation must temporarily use a specifically inactive relationship without changing the model’s default active OrderDate path.

questions.title: Do not add bidirectional filters without a requirement
questions.context: Aurora’s star schema has several dimensions connected to FactSales. All report requirements are satisfied by normal dimension-to-fact filtering, but a developer proposes setting every relationship to Both "just in case."
questions.question: What is the better design decision?

options.label: Keep single-direction dimension-to-fact filtering unless a specific scenario requires bidirectional filtering
options.explanation: Microsoft guidance recommends minimizing bidirectional relationships because they can hurt performance and create confusing or ambiguous filter paths.

options.label: Set every relationship to Both because it can only increase correctness
options.explanation: Bidirectional filtering can introduce ambiguity and performance costs; it is not automatically safer or more correct.

options.label: Remove all relationships and use DAX filters in every measure
options.explanation: Relationships are fundamental to star-schema filter propagation and should not be removed merely to avoid bidirectional filtering.

options.label: Convert every relationship to many-to-many
options.explanation: Changing cardinality would misrepresent the model when dimensions have unique keys.

questions.decisiveClue: No business requirement needs reverse filtering, so the risks of unnecessary bidirectional propagation outweigh any benefit.

questions.title: Choose Import for a small, periodically refreshed model
questions.context: Aurora has a 2-million-row sales source that changes only overnight. Users need the fastest interactive report performance during the day, and a scheduled nightly refresh is acceptable.
questions.question: Which storage mode is the strongest default choice?

options.label: Import
options.explanation: Import loads data into the semantic model’s in-memory engine, typically providing fast interactive performance when scheduled refresh latency is acceptable.

options.label: DirectQuery
options.explanation: DirectQuery keeps queries on the source at interaction time, which is unnecessary when nightly freshness is acceptable and can add source/query latency.

options.label: Direct Lake
options.explanation: Direct Lake is designed for supported OneLake Delta data; the scenario gives no OneLake requirement and already accepts a normal refresh cycle.

options.label: Live connection
options.explanation: Live connection describes connecting to an existing semantic model rather than choosing how this source table is stored in a new model.

questions.decisiveClue: The model is modest in size, freshness only needs to be nightly, and interactive performance is the priority.

questions.title: Use the required incremental-refresh parameters
questions.context: Priya is configuring incremental refresh for FactSales in Power BI Desktop and must define the date/time parameters used by the policy.
questions.question: Which parameter names are required?

options.label: RangeStart and RangeEnd
options.explanation: Incremental refresh uses the reserved, case-sensitive Power Query parameters RangeStart and RangeEnd.

options.label: StartDate and EndDate
options.explanation: These names are not the reserved parameter names expected by incremental refresh.

options.label: MinDate and MaxDate
options.explanation: These names can be meaningful custom parameters but are not the required reserved names.

options.label: From and To
options.explanation: Incremental refresh does not use these as its reserved parameter names.

questions.decisiveClue: The question asks for the reserved parameter names used by Power BI incremental refresh.

questions.title: Understand the first incremental refresh
questions.context: Aurora configures FactSales to store five years of history and refresh the last seven days. The model is published for the first time and has never been refreshed in the service.
questions.question: What is special about the first service refresh?

options.label: It creates the policy-managed partitions and loads the historical store period as well as the current refresh period
options.explanation: The first refresh establishes the incremental-refresh partition structure and loads the required historical data, so it can be much heavier than later refreshes.

options.label: It loads only seven days and permanently omits the older five-year history
options.explanation: The store policy explicitly retains five years, so the initial refresh must establish that historical data.

options.label: It creates metadata only and loads no rows until the second refresh
options.explanation: The first service refresh actually creates partitions and loads data.

options.label: It guarantees every later refresh will reload all five years
options.explanation: Subsequent refreshes normally process only the configured refresh period plus required maintenance rather than the full store period.

questions.decisiveClue: This is the model’s first service refresh after an incremental policy was defined, so historical partitions must be created and populated.

questions.title: Understand the default Direct Lake fallback setting
questions.context: Aurora uses Direct Lake on SQL endpoints. The model’s Direct Lake behavior is left at its default setting. A query encounters a documented condition that Direct Lake cannot satisfy but DirectQuery can.
questions.question: What does the default behavior do?

options.label: It silently falls back to DirectQuery for the query
options.explanation: Automatic is the default Direct Lake behavior for SQL-endpoint models and preserves functionality by allowing DirectQuery fallback when Direct Lake conditions are not met.

options.label: It always fails the query with an error instead of falling back
options.explanation: That describes DirectLakeOnly behavior when Direct Lake conditions cannot be met, not the default Automatic behavior.

options.label: It permanently converts the model to Import mode
options.explanation: Fallback changes the query path, not the model into an Import semantic model.

options.label: It permanently forces all future queries to DirectQueryOnly
options.explanation: Automatic fallback for a query does not change the model setting to DirectQueryOnly.

questions.decisiveClue: The model is Direct Lake on SQL endpoints and the behavior property remains at its default, which is Automatic.

questions.title: Diagnose fallback caused by a SQL view
questions.context: A Direct Lake on SQL endpoints model includes a table based on an unmaterialized SQL view. Performance Analyzer shows queries for the model are not staying in Direct Lake mode.
questions.question: What is the most direct explanation?

options.label: An unmaterialized SQL view is a documented DirectQuery fallback condition for Direct Lake on SQL endpoints
options.explanation: Direct Lake on SQL endpoints requires supported Delta-backed tables for Direct Lake processing; a table based on an unmaterialized SQL view causes fallback.

options.label: Any SQL view automatically converts the semantic model to Import mode
options.explanation: The documented behavior is DirectQuery fallback, not a permanent conversion to Import.

options.label: A SQL view can use Direct Lake only if semantic-model RLS is added
options.explanation: Adding semantic-model RLS does not materialize the SQL view or remove this fallback condition.

options.label: The XMLA endpoint intercepts SQL views and slows them down
options.explanation: XMLA is not the cause of the Direct Lake fallback described.

questions.decisiveClue: The model is explicitly Direct Lake on SQL endpoints and the affected table is based on an unmaterialized SQL view, a documented fallback trigger.

questions.title: Inspect the DAX generated by a slow visual
questions.context: One Aurora visual is slow. Performance Analyzer shows that most of its time is in the DAX query, and Marta wants to inspect and experiment with exactly the query that the visual generated.
questions.question: What should she do next?

options.label: Copy or run the visual’s query from Performance Analyzer in DAX query view
options.explanation: Performance Analyzer can expose the DAX query generated by a visual, and that query can be run in DAX query view for inspection and experimentation.

options.label: Open lineage view
options.explanation: Lineage helps with dependencies between items but does not expose the visual’s generated DAX query.

options.label: Deploy the report to another stage
options.explanation: Changing lifecycle stage does not isolate or inspect the DAX query causing the visual delay.

options.label: Remove sensitivity labels
options.explanation: Sensitivity labels are unrelated to DAX execution time and query inspection.

questions.decisiveClue: Performance Analyzer has already isolated the delay to the DAX query, so the next useful diagnostic is to inspect that exact generated query.
